mcqs.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes a convex lens from a concave lens?

options.A: A convex lens diverges parallel rays, while a concave lens converges them to a real focus.
options.B: A convex lens converges parallel rays to a real focus, whereas a concave lens diverges rays so that they appear to come from a virtual focus.
options.C: Both lenses converge rays to the same focal point.
options.D: Both lenses diverge rays away from the principal axis.

mcqs.answer: A convex lens converges parallel rays to a real focus, whereas a concave lens diverges rays so that they appear to come from a virtual focus.
mcqs.explanation: In a convex (converging) lens, parallel incident rays are refracted to meet at the principal focus on the opposite side, forming a real focus. In a concave (diverging) lens, parallel rays spread out after refraction; they appear to originate from a virtual focus on the same side as the object. Options A, C and D describe incorrect behaviours.

mcqs.question: The optical centre of a thin lens is the point at which:

options.A: The lens has its maximum thickness.
options.B: The lens surface is most strongly curved.
options.C: A ray passing through the lens does not change its direction.
options.D: The focal length of the lens becomes zero.

mcqs.answer: A ray passing through the lens does not change its direction.
mcqs.explanation: The optical centre is the point on the principal axis where the two refracting surfaces intersect such that a ray through this point experiences no net deviation. Options A, B and D describe unrelated properties.

mcqs.question: The principal focus of a convex lens is:

options.A: The point where diverging rays appear to originate after passing through a concave lens.
options.B: The point on the principal axis where rays parallel to the axis converge after refraction by a convex lens.
options.C: The midpoint of the lens thickness.
options.D: The point where a ray passing through the optical centre is deviated.

mcqs.answer: The point on the principal axis where rays parallel to the axis converge after refraction by a convex lens.
mcqs.explanation: For a convex (converging) lens, the principal focus (F) is where parallel rays meet after refraction. Option A describes the focus of a concave lens, while C and D are unrelated.

mcqs.question: A convex lens has a focal length of 10 cm. What is its optical power?
mcqs.explanation: Power P (in dioptres) = 1/f (in metres). f = 10 cm = 0.10 m, so P = 1/0.10 = 10 D. The other options result from incorrect conversion or inversion.

mcqs.question: An object is placed at a distance greater than twice the focal length (2F) from a convex lens. Which description correctly represents the image in the standard ray diagram?

options.A: The image is real, inverted, reduced and formed between the focal point (F) and twice the focal length (2F) on the opposite side of the lens.
options.B: The image is real, upright, enlarged and formed beyond twice the focal length on the opposite side.
options.C: The image is virtual, upright, reduced and formed between the lens and the focal point on the same side as the object.
options.D: The image is virtual, inverted, enlarged and formed exactly at twice the focal length on the opposite side.

mcqs.answer: The image is real, inverted, reduced and formed between the focal point (F) and twice the focal length (2F) on the opposite side of the lens.
mcqs.explanation: When the object is beyond 2F, the convex lens produces a real, inverted image that is smaller than the object and lies between F and 2F on the other side. Options B, C and D describe situations that correspond to other object positions or lens types.

mcqs.question: A concave lens has a focal length of –15 cm. An object is placed 30 cm in front of the lens. What are the nature and position of the image formed?

options.A: A virtual, upright, reduced image formed 10 cm in front of the lens.
options.B: A real, inverted, enlarged image formed 45 cm behind the lens.
options.C: A virtual, upright, same‑size image formed at infinity.
options.D: A real, upright, reduced image formed 10 cm behind the lens.

mcqs.answer: A virtual, upright, reduced image formed 10 cm in front of the lens.
mcqs.explanation: Using the thin‑lens formula 1/f = 1/v – 1/u (sign convention: f = –15 cm, u = –30 cm), we get v = –10 cm, indicating a virtual image 10 cm on the same side as the object. Concave lenses always produce virtual, upright, reduced images. The other options contradict the sign‑convention results or lens behaviour.

mcqs.question: A student says, “A convex lens always produces a virtual image, no matter where the object is placed.” Which statement best corrects this misconception?

options.A: The statement is correct; convex lenses never form real images.
options.B: A convex lens can produce a real image when the object is placed beyond its focal length; otherwise it forms a virtual image.
options.C: Convex lenses produce real images, while concave lenses produce virtual images, irrespective of object distance.
options.D: The type of image formed by a convex lens does not depend on the object's position.

mcqs.answer: A convex lens can produce a real image when the object is placed beyond its focal length; otherwise it forms a virtual image.
mcqs.explanation: Convex (converging) lenses form real, inverted images when the object is beyond the focal length (F) and virtual, upright images when the object is within F. Option A is false, C misattributes behaviour, and D ignores the dependence on object distance.

mcqs.question: Why does a ray that passes through the optical centre of a thin lens emerge without deviation?

options.A: Because the lens thickness is zero at that point.
options.B: Because the refractive index of the lens equals that of the surrounding medium at the optical centre.
options.C: Because at the optical centre the incident ray meets the lens surfaces such that the angles of incidence are zero, causing no deviation.
options.D: Because the optical centre coincides with the focal point of the lens.

mcqs.answer: Because at the optical centre the incident ray meets the lens surfaces such that the angles of incidence are zero, causing no deviation.
mcqs.explanation: At the optical centre the two refracting surfaces are effectively in line; a ray through this point experiences equal and opposite refractions, resulting in zero net deviation. Options A and B are incorrect statements about lens geometry and material, while D confuses the optical centre with the focal point.
